query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled preheating stage for the build substrate—raising its temperature to 200–300°C during additive manufacturing—will reduce cooling rates and thermal gradients, thereby lowering residual stresses and defect formation, which should improve both the dimensional precision and mechanical integrity of high-entropy alloy components compared to the standard process without preheating.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy components fabricated by conventional laser-based AM processes without substrate preheating, which typically exhibit high thermal gradients leading to defects such as vertical cracks, porosity, and dimensional inaccuracies.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled preheating stage to raise the substrate temperature to 200–300°C during the AM process.
generation.conditions: The intervention should be performed under optimized laser power, scanning parameters, and layer thickness in an inert atmosphere, replicating the baseline process conditions except for the introduction of substrate preheating.
generation.structural_mediator: A reduction in thermal gradients and residual stresses at the melt pool and in the deposited layers.
generation.mechanism: By preheating the substrate, the cooling rate is decreased and the temperature differential between the melt pool and the substrate is minimized. This reduction in thermal stress suppresses crack formation and other defects (e.g., porosity and lack of fusion), leading to improved microstructural uniformity and better mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The preheated process is expected to yield components with fewer fabrication-induced defects, improved dimensional accuracy, and enhanced mechanical integrity relative to components manufactured without substrate preheating.
generation.baseline: Components produced under standard additive manufacturing conditions with no substrate preheating, which suffer from higher defect density and residual stresses.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable to high-entropy alloys processed under similar laser-based AM conditions. The benefits may be limited to systems with comparable alloy compositions and may not directly translate if laser parameters, powder characteristics, or environmental conditions differ significantly.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact optimal preheating temperature within the 200–300°C range and the precise magnitude of the improvements; additional experiments are required to quantify these effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two groups of high-entropy alloy samples using identical laser parameters, scanning strategies, and environmental conditions: one group using the standard AM process without preheating and the other incorporating a substrate preheating stage at 200–300°C. Ensure that all other processing parameters remain constant.
measurements: High-resolution imaging (e.g., SEM) and defect quantification (crack density, porosity, lack of fusion)
Dimensional accuracy assessments via precise metrology
Mechanical tests (e.g., tensile, fatigue) to evaluate integrity
Thermal profiling during fabrication to verify temperature gradients
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If there is no statistically significant reduction in fabrication-induced defects, improvement in dimensional precision, or enhancement in mechanical properties in the preheated samples compared to the baseline samples, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

The Ni35Co35Cr25Ti3Al2 MEA was additively manufactured using a SLM280HL (SLM Solutions, Germany) LPBF machine equipped with a maximum power of 400 W fiber laser (spot diameter: 80 µm). Rectangular blocks with dimensions of 60 × 15 × 15 mm3 were built on a 316 L stainless steel substrate. To minimize thermal residual stresses, the build plate was pre-heated to 200 °C and maintained at this temperature throughout the process. The optimized processing parameters employed were: laser power = 320 W, scanning velocity = 1000 mm/s, hatch distance = 0.07 mm, and layer thickness = 0.03 mm, resulting in a volume energy density of about 152 J/mm3 and samples with >99.6% density. A 67° rotational scan strategy was used. The deposition process was carried out under an inert argon atmosphere with oxygen concentration below 300 ppm to minimize oxidation. After the LPBF process, the built samples were cut off from the build plate via electro-discharge machining (EDM).

cited_evidence.text: Microsections were prepared and throughout the initial investigation, samples with noteworthy lack of fusion defects or significant keyhole porosity were ruled out. In addition to these defects, large horizontal cracks were seen as critical defects, disrupting the fabrication process due to the deterioration of the thermal conductivity towards the substrate plate, as well as the possible detachment of entire sections. Therefore, the initial set of 16 samples was reduced to four samples, which exhibited large defect-free sections, and the defects present were predominantly limited to vertical cracking (Figure 6). Vertical cracks were expected due to the absence of preheating (substrate plate preheating was not employed), coupled with the larger than usual layer thickness. Raising the build space temperature to lower cooling rates and thermal gradients is the most common approach to minimize cracking. New research also suggests that high-frequency laser power modulation is a suitable approach to prevent cracking [].
